blocks.text: Perpetuity and sinking fund

Financial mathematics deals with the value of money over time. A rupee today is worth more than a rupee a year from now, because money can earn interest. Every formula below therefore uses a rate $i$ **per period**, and a count $n$ of **periods**. If the rate is quoted per year and payments are monthly, convert first: $i = \dfrac{r}{12 \times 100}$.
A sequence of equal payments made at equal intervals. An **ordinary annuity** pays at the end of each period; an annuity due pays at the beginning.

An annuity whose payments continue forever, that is, without any end date. The same amount $C$ is paid at regular intervals for ever. Examples are a scholarship fund that pays a fixed amount every year and a preference share with a fixed dividend.

$PV$ is the present value of an ordinary perpetuity, $C$ the payment made at the end of every period, and $i$ the interest rate per period in decimal form. To receive $C$ every period for ever, one must deposit $C/i$ now, because the interest alone, $i \times (C/i) = C$, pays the amount and leaves the capital untouched. For a perpetuity due (first payment today) the value is $PV = C + \dfrac{C}{i}$.

blocks.problem: A trust wants to give a scholarship of ₹2,400 every six months for ever. Interest earned is 6% per annum compounded half-yearly. How much must be deposited now (first payment after six months)?
blocks.solution: The interest rate per half-year is $i = 6\%/2 = 3\% = 0.03$, and the payment is $C = 2400$ per half-year. For an ordinary perpetuity $PV = C/i = 2400/0.03 = 80{,}000$.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: A perpetuity works because the interest on the capital, $3\%\times80{,}000=2400$, is exactly the payment, so the capital never falls. That is why $PV=C/i$ contains no number of periods.

A fund built up by making equal deposits at regular intervals, which earn compound interest, so that a required sum is available at a fixed future date, for example to repay a debt or replace an asset. Its purpose is fixed in advance, and the deposits are set aside for that purpose alone.

$A$ is the amount (future value) of the fund at the end of $n$ periods, $C$ the equal deposit made at the end of each period, $i$ the rate per period. The first form gives the final amount from known deposits; the second gives the deposit needed for a target $A$.

blocks.problem: A company wants a sinking fund of ₹5,00,000 at the end of 5 years to replace a machine. Deposits are made at the end of every year and earn 8% p.a. compounded annually. Find the annual deposit.
blocks.answer: About ₹85,228 must be deposited each year.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: Each equal deposit grows for a different number of years: the first for 4 years, the last for none. Adding the five grown amounts gives the target ₹5,00,000, which is exactly the sum that the formula $A=\dfrac{C[(1+i)^n-1]}{i}$ computes in one step.

What to learn from this figure: The fund grows faster each year because the interest (amber) is earned on a larger balance. By year 5 about ₹4,26,141 comes from the deposits and about ₹73,859 from interest.

blocks.caption: Sinking fund versus a savings account
rows: Purpose
Created for a specific future need with a target amount
General saving with no fixed target
Deposits
Fixed, regular deposits set by a plan
Deposits and withdrawals are at the holder's choice
Use of money
Not withdrawn until the target date
Can be withdrawn at any time
Interest
Compounded at the fund's rate; amount is $C[(1+i)^n-1]/i$
Interest on the changing balance, usually at a lower rate

blocks.text: Do not confuse the two annuity formulas. Perpetuity: $PV = C/i$ and it has no $n$. Sinking fund: $A = C[(1+i)^n-1]/i$, which has an end date and a **future** value. The loan formula for EMI is a **present** value formula.
EMI: equated monthly instalment

The fixed monthly payment made by a borrower to repay a loan with interest over a stated period. Every instalment is the same, which is why it is called equated. It consists of interest and part of the principal.

There are two common methods. The **flat rate method** charges interest on the whole original principal for the entire period. The **reducing balance method** charges interest only on the principal still outstanding each month, so the interest part falls and the principal part rises as the loan is repaid.
$P$ is the principal in rupees, $r$ the flat rate per annum in percent, $t$ the period in years, so $12t$ is the number of instalments. Total interest is $Prt/100$.

$E$ is the EMI by the reducing balance method, $P$ the loan amount, $i$ the monthly interest rate (decimal), $n$ the number of monthly instalments. It follows from equating the loan to the present value of the $n$ equal payments, $P = E\,\dfrac{1-(1+i)^{-n}}{i}$.

blocks.problem: A loan of ₹1,00,000 is taken at 12% p.a. for one year. Find the EMI (i) by the flat rate method and (ii) by the reducing balance method.
blocks.answer: Flat rate EMI about ₹9,333; reducing balance EMI about ₹8,885.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: Every bar has the same height, the EMI, but its colours change: the interest part (amber) shrinks each month because it is charged on the falling balance, and the principal part (blue) grows. After the 12th instalment the loan balance is zero.

For the same quoted rate, the reducing balance EMI is smaller than the flat rate EMI, because interest is charged only on what is still owed. A "flat" rate of $r\%$ is therefore effectively dearer than a reducing rate of $r\%$.

What to learn from this figure: For the same quoted 12%, the flat rate method charges ₹12,000 interest and the reducing balance method only about ₹6,619, so the flat-rate EMI is higher. The flat method takes interest on the whole principal for the whole period; the reducing method takes it only on what is still owed.
Rate of return and nominal rate of return
The gain or loss on an investment expressed as a percentage of the amount invested, taking into account any income received (dividend or interest) during the period.
$V_i$ is the initial value (cost), $V_f$ the final value (selling price or market value), $I$ the income received meanwhile. A negative value is a loss.
The rate of return measured in money terms, **without** adjusting for inflation. When inflation is allowed for, the result is the real rate of return.
An approximation valid for small rates. The exact relation is $1 + \text{real} = \dfrac{1+\text{nominal}}{1+\text{inflation}}$.

blocks.problem: A share bought for ₹500 is sold after one year for ₹560, and a dividend of ₹20 was received. Find the nominal rate of return, and the approximate real rate if inflation is 6%.
blocks.solution: Gain $= (560 - 500) + 20 = 80$. Nominal rate $= 80/500 \times 100 = 16\%$. Approximate real rate $= 16\% - 6\% = 10\%$. (The exact value is $1.16/1.06 - 1 \approx 9.43\%$.)
blocks.answer: Nominal rate of return $= 16\%$; real rate approximately $10\%$.

blocks.text: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR)
The percentage change of a quantity in a single year: $\dfrac{V_t - V_{t-1}}{V_{t-1}}\times 100\%$. It can differ greatly from year to year.

The single constant yearly rate at which a value would have had to grow, compounded each year, to go from its beginning value to its ending value in $n$ years. It smooths out the year-to-year ups and downs.
$V_i$ is the beginning value, $V_f$ the ending value, $n$ the number of years (the number of growth steps, not the number of data points). Multiply by 100 for a percentage.

blocks.problem: A value moves from 100 to 120 in year 1 and then to 108 in year 2. Find the annual growth rates and the CAGR.
blocks.answer: Growth rates $+20\%$ and $-10\%$; CAGR $\approx 3.92\%$ per year.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: The plain average of $+20\%$ and $-10\%$ is $5\%$, but growing 5% twice gives $110.25$, not the actual $108$. The CAGR of about $3.92\%$ is the constant yearly rate that really takes 100 to 108 in two years.

CAGR is not the arithmetic average of annual growth rates. For rates $+20\%$ and $-10\%$ the average is $5\%$ but the true compound rate is only about $3.92\%$. Also remember the exponent is $1/n$, with $n$ equal to the number of years between the two values.
Linear method of depreciation
The fall in the value of an asset due to use, wear and passage of time, treated as a yearly expense.

blocks.term: Cost, residual value and useful life
blocks.text: **Cost** is the original purchase price (including installation). **Residual (scrap) value** is the amount the asset is expected to fetch at the end of its life. **Useful life** is the number of years the asset is expected to be used.

$D$ is the equal depreciation charged every year by the linear (straight-line) method, and $V_t$ the book value after $t$ years. The book value falls on a straight line and reaches the residual value at the end of the useful life.

blocks.problem: A machine costs ₹1,20,000, has a useful life of 8 years and a residual value of ₹20,000. Find the yearly depreciation and the book value after 5 years.
blocks.answer: Depreciation ₹12,500 per year; book value after 5 years ₹57,500.

blocks.text: What to learn from this figure: Straight-line depreciation takes the same amount off each year, so the book value falls along a straight line from the cost to the residual value at the end of the useful life. The yearly amount uses (cost $-$ residual value), not the full cost.
In the linear method the depreciation is the same every year and is charged on the amount (Cost $-$ Residual value), not on the full cost.
Valuation of bonds
A debt instrument in which the issuer borrows money from investors and promises to pay a fixed interest (coupon) at regular intervals and to repay the face value on a fixed maturity date.

blocks.caption: Terms related to bonds
rows: Face (par) value $F$
Amount printed on the bond, repaid at maturity
Coupon rate
Annual interest as a percentage of face value; coupon payment $C = F \times \text{coupon rate}$
Maturity
The date (or number of years $n$) at which the face value is repaid
Redemption value
Amount actually paid to the holder at maturity (often equal to face value)
Yield / market rate $i$
The rate of return investors require, used for discounting

blocks.text: $V$ is the value (price) of the bond today by the present value approach: the coupons are discounted as an annuity and the redemption value is discounted as a single sum. $i$ is the market rate per period.

blocks.problem: A bond of face value ₹1,000 pays a coupon of 8% every year for 3 years and is redeemed at par. If investors require 10%, find its value.
blocks.solution: The coupon paid at the end of each of the three years is the coupon rate times the face value. Coupon $C = 8\% \times 1000 = 80$. $V = \dfrac{80}{1.1} + \dfrac{80}{1.1^2} + \dfrac{80 + 1000}{1.1^3} = 72.73 + 66.12 + 811.42 = 950.26$.
blocks.answer: Value of the bond $\approx$ ₹950.26, which is below its face value.

blocks.text: If the required yield is higher than the coupon rate, the bond is worth less than its face value (it sells at a discount). If the yield equals the coupon rate, the value equals the face value. If the yield is lower, the bond sells at a premium.

What to learn from this figure: The bond price falls as the required yield rises. At 8%, equal to the coupon rate, the price is the face value, ₹1,000. At 10% it is about ₹950.26 (a discount) and at 6% about ₹1,053.46 (a premium).

questions.stem: A perpetuity is an annuity in which
options: payments of a fixed amount continue for ever
payments stop after a fixed number of years
only one lump sum is paid at the end
the payment amount doubles every year
questions.explanation: A perpetuity is a never-ending series of equal payments made at regular intervals, such as a scholarship that pays a fixed sum every year. Because it never ends, its present value is the finite quantity $C/i$.

optionRationale.2: This describes an ordinary annuity with a finite term.
optionRationale.3: That is a single payment, not a series of payments.
optionRationale.4: A perpetuity has equal payments, not growing ones.

questions.objective: Define perpetuity

questions.stem: The present value of a perpetuity of ₹5,000 paid at the end of every year, when the interest rate is 10% per annum, is
questions.explanation: For an ordinary perpetuity $PV = C/i = 5000/0.10 = 50{,}000$. Check by reversing the calculation: the interest on ₹50,000 at 10% is exactly ₹5,000 each year, so the capital stays intact and the payment can be made for ever without using it up.

optionRationale.1: This is just one payment, not the value of all future payments.
optionRationale.4: This adds one payment to the present value, which would apply to a perpetuity due.

questions.objective: Calculate present value of a perpetuity

questions.stem: The main purpose of a sinking fund is to
options: borrow money at a low rate of interest
accumulate a required sum by a fixed future date through regular deposits
pay interest on a perpetual bond
questions.explanation: A sinking fund collects equal periodic deposits that earn compound interest, so that a known amount is available on a set date, for repaying a debenture or replacing an asset. The money is earmarked for that purpose.

optionRationale.1: A sinking fund is a store of deposits, not a loan.
optionRationale.3: Perpetuities are separate; the sinking fund aims at a target amount.
optionRationale.4: Depreciation is a different calculation; a sinking fund may only finance replacement.

questions.objective: Explain the concept of a sinking fund

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A sinking fund differs from an ordinary savings account.
Reason (R): A sinking fund is built with regular deposits for a specific purpose and a target amount on a fixed date, while a savings account has no fixed target and money can be withdrawn at any time.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The sinking fund is planned: fixed deposits, a purpose, and a target amount on a set date. A savings account is flexible and goal-free. The reason lists exactly this difference, so it correctly explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: The reason states the actual differences, so it is the explanation.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: a savings account allows withdrawals at any time.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: the two serve different purposes.

questions.objective: Differentiate sinking fund and savings account

questions.stem: An asset costing ₹50,000 has a residual value of ₹5,000 and a useful life of 5 years. By the linear method the annual depreciation is
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation $D = (\text{Cost} - \text{Residual value})/\text{Useful life} = (50{,}000 - 5{,}000)/5 = 45{,}000/5 = 9{,}000$. It is the same every year under the linear method.

optionRationale.2: This divides the full cost by the life and ignores the residual value.
optionRationale.3: This adds the residual value instead of subtracting it: $(50{,}000+5{,}000)/5$.
optionRationale.4: This is the total depreciable amount, not the yearly charge.

questions.objective: Compute linear depreciation

questions.stem: A perpetuity pays ₹2,400 at the end of every half-year. If money earns 6% per annum compounded half-yearly, its present value is
questions.explanation: The rate per period is the half-yearly rate $6\%/2 = 3\% = 0.03$ and the payment per period is ₹2,400. $PV = C/i = 2400/0.03 = 80{,}000$. The period of the rate must match the period of the payment.

optionRationale.1: This uses the annual rate $6\%$ with the half-yearly payment: $2400/0.06$.
optionRationale.3: This uses $i = 1.5\%$, which is too small; the half-year rate is $3\%$.
optionRationale.4: This adds the first payment to the value, as for a perpetuity due.

questions.objective: Match the rate with the payment period in a perpetuity

questions.stem: A sinking fund of ₹5,00,000 is to be built in 5 years with equal deposits at the end of each year, earning 8% p.a. compounded annually. Using $(1.08)^5 = 1.469328$, the annual deposit is approximately
questions.explanation: Deposit $C = \dfrac{A\,i}{(1+i)^n - 1} = \dfrac{5{,}00{,}000 \times 0.08}{0.469328} = \dfrac{40{,}000}{0.469328} \approx 85{,}228$. It is below ₹1,00,000 because the deposits themselves earn interest.

optionRationale.2: This applies the loan (present value) formula $A\,i/(1-(1+i)^{-n})$ to a future value.
optionRationale.3: This is the interest for one year on the target amount, $0.08 \times 5{,}00{,}000$.

questions.objective: Calculate the periodic deposit of a sinking fund

questions.stem: A loan of ₹1,00,000 is repaid in equal monthly instalments over 2 years with interest at 10% per annum on the whole principal (flat rate). The EMI is
questions.explanation: Interest $= 1{,}00{,}000 \times 10 \times 2/100 = 20{,}000$, so the total to repay is ₹1,20,000. The number of instalments is $12 \times 2 = 24$, so EMI $= 1{,}20{,}000/24 = 5{,}000$.

optionRationale.3: This adds only one year of interest: $(1{,}00{,}000+10{,}000)/24$.

questions.objective: Calculate EMI by the flat rate method

questions.stem: A loan of ₹1,00,000 at 12% p.a. is repaid in 12 equal monthly instalments by the reducing balance method. Using $(1.01)^{12} = 1.126825$, the EMI is approximately
questions.explanation: The monthly rate is $i = 12/1200 = 0.01$ and $n = 12$. $E = \dfrac{P\,i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1} = \dfrac{1000 \times 1.126825}{0.126825} \approx 8{,}885$. It is less than the flat rate EMI of ₹9,333.

optionRationale.3: This is the flat rate EMI, which charges interest on the whole principal.
optionRationale.4: This is not obtained from the formula and has no basis.

questions.objective: Calculate EMI by the reducing balance method

questions.stem: A share bought for ₹500 is sold after one year for ₹560 and a dividend of ₹20 is received. The nominal rate of return is
questions.explanation: Total gain $= (560 - 500) + 20 = 80$. The nominal rate of return $= 80/500 \times 100 = 16\%$. It is called nominal because no adjustment for inflation has been made, so the purchasing power lost to rising prices is not deducted from it.

optionRationale.4: This is $(560-500-20)/500$, subtracting the dividend instead of adding it.

questions.objective: Calculate the nominal rate of return

questions.stem: An investment of ₹10,000 grows to ₹14,641 in 4 years. Its compound annual growth rate is
questions.explanation: CAGR $= (V_f/V_i)^{1/n} - 1 = (14{,}641/10{,}000)^{1/4} - 1 = (1.4641)^{1/4} - 1 = 1.1 - 1 = 10\%$, since $1.1^4 = 1.4641$. The exponent is one fourth because growth took place over four years, and the answer is a yearly compound rate, not the total growth of 46.41%.

optionRationale.2: This is the simple average $46.41\%/4$ of the total growth.
optionRationale.3: This is the total growth over four years, not a yearly rate.
optionRationale.4: This does not reproduce the final value: $10{,}000 \times 1.12^4 \approx 15{,}735$.

questions.objective: Calculate CAGR

questions.stem: Match each concept in List-I with its description in List-II.
questions.explanation: A perpetuity is an endless annuity (A-III). A sinking fund accumulates deposits to a future target (B-I). An EMI is the fixed monthly loan repayment (C-II). CAGR is the constant yearly growth rate between two values (D-IV).

optionRationale.1: This swaps the descriptions of perpetuity and sinking fund.
optionRationale.3: This swaps sinking fund and EMI.

questions.objective: Match financial mathematics terms

right: I. Equal deposits that accumulate to a target sum on a future date
II. A fixed monthly payment that repays a loan with interest
III. An annuity whose payments never end
IV. The constant yearly rate that takes a beginning value to an ending value

questions.stem: A machine costing ₹1,20,000 has a residual value of ₹20,000 and a useful life of 8 years. Its book value after 5 years by the linear method is
questions.explanation: Annual depreciation is $(1{,}20{,}000 - 20{,}000)/8 = 12{,}500$. After 5 years the total depreciation is $62{,}500$, so the book value is $1{,}20{,}000 - 62{,}500 = 57{,}500$.

optionRationale.1: This is the accumulated depreciation after 5 years, not the book value.
optionRationale.4: This is the residual value, which is reached only at the end of the 8th year.

questions.objective: Find book value under the linear method

questions.stem: A sinking fund receives ₹10,000 at the end of each year for 3 years and earns 10% p.a. compounded annually. The amount in the fund at the end of the third year is
questions.explanation: $A = C\,\dfrac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i} = 10{,}000 \times \dfrac{1.331 - 1}{0.1} = 10{,}000 \times 3.31 = 33{,}100$. Equivalently, the first deposit earns interest for two years, the second for one year and the last for none, so $10{,}000(1.21 + 1.1 + 1) = 33{,}100$.

optionRationale.3: This treats deposits as made at the beginning of each year, with an extra year of interest.
optionRationale.4: This adds a simple ₹1,000 of interest on each deposit instead of compounding.

questions.objective: Find the amount of a sinking fund

questions.stem: The values of an investment are 100 at the start, 120 after year 1 and 108 after year 2. The CAGR over the two years is approximately
questions.explanation: CAGR $= (108/100)^{1/2} - 1 = \sqrt{1.08} - 1 \approx 1.0392 - 1 = 3.92\%$. Check: $100 \times 1.0392^2 \approx 108$. Annual growth rates were $+20\%$ and $-10\%$, and averaging them gives the wrong value of $5\%$.

optionRationale.1: This is the simple average of $+20\%$ and $-10\%$, which is not a compound rate.
optionRationale.3: This is $8\%/2$, the total growth divided by two years.
optionRationale.4: This is the total growth over two years, not a yearly rate.

questions.objective: Differentiate CAGR from annual growth rate

questions.stem: A bond of face value ₹1,000 pays a 8% coupon every year for 3 years and is redeemed at par. If investors require a yield of 10%, its present value is approximately
questions.explanation: $V = 80/1.1 + 80/1.21 + 1080/1.331 = 72.73 + 66.12 + 811.42 = 950.26$. Because the required yield (10%) exceeds the coupon rate (8%), the value is below the face value, so the bond sells at a discount to its face value of ₹1,000.

optionRationale.1: The value equals the face value only if the yield equals the coupon rate.
optionRationale.2: This discounts all cash flows $(240+1000)$ as if received at the end of year 3.
optionRationale.3: A bond sells above par only when the required yield is below the coupon rate.

questions.objective: Value a bond by the present value approach

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): A bond whose coupon rate is lower than the required market yield has a present value below its face value.
Reason (R): The coupons and the face value are discounted at the market yield, and the coupons are smaller than what the market yield demands.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The bond pays a coupon below the return investors require, so to give them the required yield the price must fall below the face value. In the formula, discounting at the higher market rate lowers $V$ below $F$, which is what the reason explains.

optionRationale.2: The reason states the cause of the discount, so it explains the assertion.
optionRationale.3: The reason is true: valuation discounts all cash flows at the market yield.
optionRationale.4: The assertion is true: for example, an 8% bond at a 10% yield is worth about ₹950.26.

questions.objective: Relate coupon rate, yield and bond value

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. The present value of an ordinary perpetuity is $C/i$.
B. The EMI by the reducing balance method is smaller than the flat rate EMI for the same quoted rate and period.
C. CAGR is always equal to the arithmetic average of the annual growth rates.
D. In the linear method the yearly depreciation equals (Cost $-$ Residual value) divided by the useful life.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The perpetuity value is $C/i$ (A). Reducing balance charges interest only on the outstanding principal, so its EMI is smaller than the flat rate EMI (B). Linear depreciation is $(\text{Cost}-\text{Residual})/\text{Life}$ (D). CAGR differs from the arithmetic mean of growth rates (C false).

optionRationale.2: Statement C is false: CAGR is a compound rate and differs from the simple average whenever growth rates vary.
optionRationale.3: C is false and A is also true.
optionRationale.4: B is also correct, so this selection is incomplete.

questions.objective: Judge statements across financial mathematics

questions.stem: An investment gives a nominal rate of return of 16% in a year when inflation is 6%. Using the approximation real rate $\approx$ nominal rate $-$ inflation rate, the real rate of return is
questions.explanation: The real rate adjusts the nominal return for the loss of purchasing power caused by inflation. By the approximation, $16\% - 6\% = 10\%$. The exact figure is $1.16/1.06 - 1 \approx 9.43\%$, which shows the approximation is reasonable for small rates.

optionRationale.1: This adds inflation to the nominal rate instead of subtracting it.
optionRationale.2: This is the nominal rate itself and ignores the loss of purchasing power.
optionRationale.4: This is $16\% \times 0.6$, which has no basis in the relation.

questions.stem: A loan is repaid in 24 equal monthly instalments of ₹5,500 under a flat rate of 10% p.a. over 2 years. The loan amount was
questions.explanation: Total repaid $= 5{,}500 \times 24 = 1{,}32{,}000$. Under the flat rate method total repayment $= P(1 + 10 \times 2/100) = 1.2P$. So $P = 1{,}32{,}000/1.2 = 1{,}10{,}000$.

optionRationale.1: This is the total repaid, $5{,}500 \times 24$, including interest.
optionRationale.2: This is the loan for an EMI of ₹5,000.
optionRationale.3: This is $1{,}10{,}000 	imes 1.1$, an unjustified extra $10%$.
